{{Short description|Method of testing for the convergence of an infinite series}}
{{Calculus|Series}}

In [[mathematics]], the '''limit comparison test (LCT)''' (in contrast with the related [[direct comparison test]]) is a method of testing for the convergence of an [[infinite series]].

== Statement ==

Suppose that we have two series <math> \Sigma_n a_n </math> and <math>\Sigma_n b_n</math> with <math> a_n\geq 0, b_n > 0 </math> for all <math> n</math>.
Then if <math> \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{a_n}{b_n} = c</math> with <math> 0 < c < \infty </math>, then either both series converge or both series diverge.<ref>{{citation|first=Earl|last=Swokowski|title=Calculus with analytic geometry|edition=Alternate|year=1983|publisher=Prindle, Weber & Schmidt|isbn=0-87150-341-7|page=[https://archive.org/details/calculuswithanal00swok/page/516 516]|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/calculuswithanal00swok/page/516}}</ref>

== Proof ==

Because <math> \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{a_n}{b_n} = c</math> we know that for every <math> \varepsilon > 0 </math> there is a positive integer <math>n_0</math> such that for all <math>n \geq n_0 </math> we have that <math> \left| \frac{a_n}{b_n} - c \right| < \varepsilon </math>, or equivalently

: <math> - \varepsilon < \frac{a_n}{b_n} - c < \varepsilon </math>

: <math> c - \varepsilon < \frac{a_n}{b_n} < c + \varepsilon </math>

: <math> (c - \varepsilon)b_n < a_n < (c + \varepsilon)b_n </math>
As <math> c > 0 </math> we can choose <math> \varepsilon </math> to be sufficiently small such that <math> c-\varepsilon </math> is positive.
So <math> b_n < \frac{1}{c-\varepsilon} a_n </math> and by the [[direct comparison test]], if <math>\sum_n a_n</math> converges then so does <math>\sum_n b_n </math>.

Similarly <math> a_n < (c + \varepsilon)b_n </math>, so if <math> \sum_n a_n </math> diverges, again by the direct comparison test, so does <math>\sum_n b_n </math>.

That is, both series converge or both series diverge.

==Example==

We want to determine if the series <math> \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2 + 2n} </math> converges.  For this we compare it with the convergent series <math> \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2} = \frac{\pi^2}{6} </math>

As <math> \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n^2 + 2n} \frac{n^2}{1} = 1 > 0 </math> we have that the original series also converges.

== One-sided version ==

One can state a one-sided comparison test by using [[limit superior]]. Let <math> a_n, b_n \geq 0 </math> for all <math> n</math>. Then if <math> \limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{a_n}{b_n} = c</math> with <math> 0 \leq c < \infty </math> and <math>\Sigma_n b_n</math> converges, necessarily <math> \Sigma_n a_n </math> converges.

== Example ==

Let <math> a_n = \frac{1-(-1)^n}{n^2} </math> and <math> b_n = \frac{1}{n^2} </math> for all natural numbers <math> n </math>. Now 
<math> \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{a_n}{b_n} = \lim_{n\to\infty}(1-(-1)^n) </math> does not exist, so we cannot apply the standard comparison test. However, 
<math> \limsup_{n\to\infty} \frac{a_n}{b_n} = \limsup_{n\to\infty}(1-(-1)^n) =2\in [0,\infty) </math> and since <math>\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2}</math> converges, the one-sided comparison test implies that <math>\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1-(-1)^n}{n^2}</math> converges.

== Converse of the one-sided comparison test ==

Let <math> a_n, b_n \geq 0 </math> for all <math> n</math>. If <math>\Sigma_n a_n </math> diverges and <math>\Sigma_n b_n </math> converges, then necessarily 
<math> \limsup_{n\to\infty} \frac{a_n}{b_n}=\infty </math>, that is, 
<math> \liminf_{n\to\infty} \frac{b_n}{a_n}= 0 </math>. The essential content here is that in some sense the numbers <math> a_n </math> are larger than the numbers <math> b_n </math>.

== Example ==

Let <math> f(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_nz^n </math> be analytic in the unit disc <math>D = \{ z\in\mathbb{C} : |z|<1\}</math> and have image of finite area. By [[Parseval's formula]] the area of the image of <math> f </math> is proportional to <math> \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n|a_n|^2</math>. Moreover, 
<math> \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} 1/n</math> diverges. Therefore, by the converse of the comparison test, we have
<math> \liminf_{n\to\infty} \frac{n|a_n|^2}{1/n}= \liminf_{n\to\infty} (n|a_n|)^2 = 0 </math>, that is,
<math> \liminf_{n\to\infty} n|a_n| = 0 </math>.
